open-question.question: What do the installation docs say to a user whose project still holds a .agents/plugins/cairn/ copy extracted under an earlier release, which the host would discover beside the global copy — an instruction to remove it, a statement that a workspace-local copy is unsupported, or nothing?
open-question.applied-principle: Check tier claims against the live environment
open-question.recommendation: The host's own plugin guide states that plugin names share one global namespace and that when two plugins claim the same name the first discovered wins and the other is dropped silently, so a stale workspace copy can shadow the global one with the agents that lack write tools; one pasteable removal command closes that off without claiming which copy wins and without a probe the guide already answers.
open-question.alternative: The README's Antigravity installation section (the template under scripts/hosts/antigravity/ and the root README.md that carries it word for word) gains a short note for projects that extracted cairn under an earlier release: remove the project's .agents/plugins/cairn/ directory, with the literal command to do so and one clause on why (the old copy is discovered beside the global one, and it predates the subagents' write and shell tools). The note says nothing about how the host ranks or merges the two copies. Gives the one concrete action that removes the risk. A stale 1.8.5-or-earlier copy carries the agent files without enable_write_tools, so if the host loads it the user hits exactly the reported failure again. A command they can paste closes that off without needing to know how the host chooses between duplicates. Puts a destructive command in the install docs that every new reader sees, even though it only applies to projects that installed before this release. It also tells users to act on behaviour nobody has checked: how agy handles two plugins both named cairn, one global and one in .agents/plugins/, was not part of any hands-on check.

The README's Antigravity installation section states that the global ~/.gemini/config/plugins/cairn copy is the only supported installation and that a workspace-local .agents/plugins/cairn/ copy is unsupported. It gives no command and no removal instruction, and says nothing about how the host treats the two copies together. Draws the support line in one declarative sentence that stays true however agy ranks duplicate plugins. Bug reports from a project that still holds an old copy can be pointed back at that sentence, and the docs gain no destructive command. Leaves the user to work out that "unsupported" means "delete it", and that the old copy may be why subagents fail. Someone who skims past it can keep running a copy without write tools, see the reported FAILED: subagents, and get no hint of the cause.

This milestone first checks by hand what agy 1.4.0 does when a workspace holds a .agents/plugins/cairn/ copy beside the global one: whether it loads both, prefers one, or reports a conflict through agy plugin list. The README's Antigravity section then states the observed result and the action that follows from it, which is a removal instruction if the workspace copy is loaded or shadows the global one, and no note if the host ignores it. Bases the docs on what the host actually does rather than on an assumed conflict. The note is written only when it is needed, and when it is, it can say exactly what the user will see, so it holds no guess about precedence and no warning against a problem that doesn't exist. Adds one more hands-on probe to the milestone and makes the README wording depend on its outcome, so the docs task can't be written until the probe has run. The observed behaviour is pinned to one agy version and can drift on a later release without the note being rechecked.

The README's installation section describes only the fresh global install and says nothing about earlier copies. The advice to remove a project's .agents/plugins/cairn/ copy goes into the CHANGELOG.md entry for the release that moves the path, which /release-plugin writes at release time, so it reaches the people who are upgrading. Puts the migration advice where upgrading users look and keeps the install section clean for the far larger set of new readers. Once the release is old, the advice sits in history instead of lingering as a permanent caveat in the README. The milestone itself writes nothing, so whether the advice lands depends on the release step picking it up from the milestone's commits. A user who reinstalls from the README months later without reading the changelog never sees it.

The installation docs say nothing about workspace-local copies, now or later. The Antigravity section shows only the global extract command, and a project that still holds a .agents/plugins/cairn/ copy is left as it is. Keeps the docs to the one install path and adds no wording that depends on unverified host behaviour. The Antigravity tree has had few installs, so few projects, perhaps only the maintainer's own, are likely to hold an old copy at all. Any project that does hold an old copy is left exposed to the exact failure this milestone fixes: the host may load the stale agents, which lack enable_write_tools, and nothing in the docs points to the leftover directory as the cause.

open-question.question: Does the README's Antigravity installation section, now extracting into ~/.gemini/config/plugins/cairn once per machine rather than once per project, tell the user that the host discovers a new plugin directory only on startup and that a running agy session must be restarted after the extract, or does it keep to the extract command alone?
open-question.applied-principle: Check tier claims against the live environment
open-question.recommendation: States only what the host's plugin guide documents, that a newly installed plugin directory is discovered on startup, heading off the likeliest first-run failure of a once-per-machine install in one sentence kept identical in both README copies; the update case is undocumented and stays out, and a listing command would show the copy installed, not loaded.
open-question.alternative: Both the README template and the root README.md follow the extract command with one sentence: Antigravity discovers a new plugin directory only on startup, so restart any agy session that was running during the extract. The note covers the first install only and says nothing about re-extracting a newer release over an existing global copy. It states exactly what agy's built-in plugin guide documents, a new directory found only on startup, and nothing more. One sentence heads off the likeliest first-run failure (cairn missing from the session that is already open) without claiming any unverified behaviour. It says nothing about updates. Whether skills changed by re-extracting over an existing ~/.gemini/config/plugins/cairn take effect in a running session is not documented or verified, so a user updating mid-session may still run stale skill text. It also adds a host-behaviour claim to the README that has to be kept true if agy changes.

The Antigravity installation section in both the README template (scripts/hosts/antigravity/README.md) and the root README.md gets only the new global target: a mkdir -p and the curl | tar extract into ~/.gemini/config/plugins/cairn, with the template's existing paragraph on pinning a release by tag kept. Nothing is said about startup discovery or restarting a running agy session, for a first install or for an update. The section stays parallel to the Claude Code and Codex sections, which carry no restart or reload note, and the README states nothing about host behaviour beyond what the extract does, so there is no sentence to go stale if a later agy release starts discovering plugins while running. The CLI's own plugin guide says a new plugin directory is discovered only on startup, so a user who extracts while an agy session is open finds no /cairn: skills there and has no hint why. The move to a once-per-machine install makes that more likely, since the user is now installing outside any one project's session.

Both the README template and the root README.md follow the extract command with a note covering every extract: restart any running agy session after installing, and again after re-extracting a newer or pinned release over the global copy, because the host reads the plugin's directory and skills at startup. One rule covers both the first install and every update, including the tag-pinning path the template already describes. A user never runs a session that mixes the old skill text with the new tool files. The update half goes beyond what the host documents, which is that a new directory is discovered only on startup. Unless this milestone's hands-on check confirms it, the README asserts reload behaviour nobody has verified, and the restart it asks for after an update may be unnecessary.

Both the README template and the root README.md follow the extract command with the first-install restart sentence (a new plugin directory is discovered only on startup, so restart a running agy session) plus a verification command, agy plugin list, which should show cairn enabled at ~/.gemini/config/plugins/cairn. Updates are not addressed. The user can confirm that the global copy landed where the host looks, which is the exact failure the milestone fixes, the orchestrator not finding the plugin at the path it expected. And the restart sentence covers the one case where the copy is in place but the open session cannot see it. It adds a second command and ties the README to the agy plugin list output and its subcommand name, which no other host's section does and which a CLI change can make wrong. A listing shows the plugin is installed, not that the running session has loaded it, so the restart sentence is still what fixes the open-session case.

alternative.id: Restart note in host README only

open-question.alternative: The first-install restart sentence follows the extract command only in the README template, which renders into the cairn-antigravity distribution repository's landing page. The root README.md's Antigravity section keeps to the extract command into ~/.gemini/config/plugins/cairn alone. The root README stays a terse install index whose host sections all have the same shape, and the host-specific detail lives on the page an Antigravity user lands on when installing from that host's distribution repository. The two sections, which today carry the same install command, drift apart, and a user who installs from the root README, the project's main landing page, never sees the note. Keeping two copies of one section in lockstep becomes a judgment call rather than a copy.

open-question.question: Does the milestone correct the sentence in docs/ways-of-using-cairn.md stating that an agy run loads the plugin from its working directory, which the global install makes false, or is the documentation change limited to the README's Antigravity installation section and the host definition's own comments?
open-question.recommendation: Only four tracked user-facing statements name the workspace-local path or say the plugin loads from the working directory (the two install sections, the distribution README's opening sentence, the bug form's manifest location, and the headless-chains bullet), each a one-sentence edit, so leaving any of them ships a release whose own documents contradict where it installs.
open-question.alternative: The milestone corrects every tracked, non-historical statement that names the workspace-local plugin path or says the plugin loads from the working directory: the two installation sections and the host definition's comments, the --add-dir bullet in docs/ways-of-using-cairn.md, the Antigravity manifest location in .github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/bug.yml (to ~/.gemini/config/plugins/cairn/plugin.json), and the opening sentence of the scripts/hosts/antigravity/README.md template that describes extraction into a workspace's .agents/plugins/cairn/. CHANGELOG.md entries and finished milestones' files stay as written, being records of past releases. Leaves no tracked surface a user reads — headless-chain guide, bug form, distribution landing page — naming a path the release no longer installs to, so the global location is the one place every document points. Widens the milestone's documentation diff to files outside the installation sections, including the issue template and the distribution README intro, each of which must be reworded and reviewed; what the reworded text says about a leftover workspace-local copy depends on the sibling question on stale workspace-local copies.

The documentation change stays limited to the Antigravity installation section of the root README.md and of the scripts/hosts/antigravity/README.md template, plus the host definition's own comments; the docs/ways-of-using-cairn.md sentence saying an agy run loads the plugin from its working directory is left as it stands, and so is every other tracked mention of the workspace-local path (the bug issue template's manifest location, the distribution README's opening sentence about extraction into a workspace's .agents/plugins/cairn/). Keeps the milestone's documentation diff to the two installation sections the goal names, with nothing outside the install path and host definition to review or keep in step. Ships a release whose own docs contradict it: the headless-chain page tells an agy user the plugin is loaded from the project's working directory, and the bug template and distribution README intro point at a .agents/plugins/cairn path the global install no longer uses, so a user following them looks in the wrong place.

Beyond the two installation sections and the host definition's comments, the milestone rewrites the --add-dir bullet in docs/ways-of-using-cairn.md so it no longer says an agy run loads the plugin from its working directory: the run still takes its working directory as its workspace and works on the project there, while the plugin comes from the global install. Other tracked mentions of the workspace-local path (the bug issue template's manifest location, the distribution README's opening sentence) are left unchanged. Corrects the one statement outside the installation sections that describes how an agy run behaves at runtime, the one a headless-chain user acts on, with a one-sentence edit and no wider sweep. Leaves two other stale references in place: the bug report form still asks Antigravity users for the version at .agents/plugins/cairn/plugin.json, and the published distribution README still says its tree is laid out for extraction into a workspace's .agents/plugins/cairn/, both of which name a path a globally installed user does not have.

open-question.question: Where does the on-demand agy suite live and how is it kept out of uv run pytest and the CI job — a marked module under tests/ that a default addopts deselects and an explicit marker selects, a directory outside pytest's testpaths that is run by naming its path, or a standalone script outside pytest invoked directly — given that the default run must stay unchanged on a machine with no agy?
open-question.recommendation: Its location alone keeps both default runs and CI byte-for-byte unchanged, with no config line, naming convention, or environment variable to hold, while keeping pytest's fixtures, reporting, and per-test selection; the suite needs its own fixtures (seeded repositories, an agy launcher) rather than the tool suite's, so a separate conftest costs nothing it would have reused.
open-question.alternative: The suite is a pytest directory outside testpaths (for example agy_tests/ at the repository root), with its own conftest.py. testpaths = ["tests"] and the CI workflow stay as they are, so uv run pytest and the floor run never reach it. It is invoked by naming the directory: uv run pytest agy_tests. Where the suite sits says that it is excluded, so no config line, file-name convention, or environment variable has to hold. Both default runs are byte-for-byte unchanged, and the suite can grow its own fixtures (temporary workspaces, agy invocation helpers) without touching the tool suite's conftest. It adds a new top-level directory to the recorded repository layout and cannot use tests/conftest.py's fixtures without importing across directories or duplicating them. A contributor running pytest on the whole repository (uv run pytest .) would collect it.

The suite is a pytest module under tests/ (for example tests/test_agy.py) whose tests carry an agy marker. pyproject.toml's [tool.pytest.ini_options] registers the marker and gains addopts = -m "not agy", so uv run pytest and the 3.9 floor run (which reads the same pyproject.toml config) deselect it. It is invoked as uv run pytest -m agy, whose -m overrides the addopts one. It is the standard pytest idiom for opt-in tests. The suite lives in the one tests/ directory beside the existing modules, keeps the flat test_<name>.py naming, and reuses tests/conftest.py's REPO_ROOT, tool paths, and fixtures directly. The default runs do not stay fully unchanged. pyproject.toml's pytest config gains its first addopts and marker, both default runs (CI included) still import and collect the module and report it as deselected, so the module must import cleanly under 3.9 on a machine with no agy. And any later -m expression a contributor passes replaces the deselection and can pull the agy tests in.

The suite is a pytest module under tests/ whose file name falls outside pytest's default test_*.py collection pattern (for example tests/agy_suite.py). With testpaths = ["tests"] unchanged and no addopts, uv run pytest never collects it, while pytest collects any file named explicitly on its command line whatever its name. It is invoked by naming its path: uv run pytest tests/agy_suite.py. Nothing changes in pyproject.toml, the CI workflow, or what either default run imports or reports, so a machine with no agy sees exactly today's run. The module still shares tests/conftest.py and its fixtures. The exclusion rests only on an unstated naming convention. A later rename to the test_ prefix, or a python_files change, silently puts agy-driving tests into CI and the default run with nothing to catch it. It also breaks the repository's recorded "one flat test_<name>.py per concern" layout for tests/.

The suite is a pytest module under tests/ (for example tests/test_agy.py), and tests/conftest.py adds it to collect_ignore unless an opt-in environment variable (for example CAIRN_AGY=1) is set. Unset, the module is not collected, so neither default run imports or reports it. pyproject.toml is unchanged. It is invoked as CAIRN_AGY=1 uv run pytest tests/test_agy.py, or with the bare uv run pytest under the variable. The exclusion is an explicit, coded switch that a rename cannot defeat, and the default runs neither collect nor mention the module. The suite keeps the flat test_ naming, the shared conftest fixtures, and pyproject.toml's config untouched. It adds a conditional collection rule and a new environment-variable name to tests/conftest.py, which until now holds only fixtures. Invoking the suite means remembering a variable rather than a pytest option or a path. And a variable left exported in a maintainer's shell quietly turns every later default run into a slow agy run.

The suite is a self-contained Python script outside pytest entirely (for example scripts/agy_suite.py beside build_hosts.py and set_version.py), invoked directly as uv run scripts/agy_suite.py or python3 scripts/agy_suite.py. It drives each agy -p process, checks its own pass conditions, prints its own per-check report, and signals the outcome through its exit status. No pytest file, marker, config line, or collection rule is involved. No pytest configuration or discovery path can ever reach the suite, so the default runs and CI are untouched by construction. It sits with the other maintainer-invoked scripts that are run by name, and a prerequisite check can stop the whole run cleanly before any agy process starts. It gives up pytest's assertion reporting, tmp_path and fixtures, and per-test selection, so the script must hand-roll its own checks, temporary workspaces, and summary. It also puts a test harness into a directory that today holds only build and release tooling. How it handles a missing agy is owned by the sibling question on running without agy, which this option's shape constrains to a whole-run stop or a hand-written skip.

open-question.question: How does the agy suite exercise a subagent's write and shell tools and what signal does it accept as a pass — a full /cairn:provide-alternatives-to-all-open-questions run on a fixture milestone, passing when the alternatives land in open_questions.xml and its commit, or a minimal headless prompt that dispatches the agent directly with a trivial write-and-run task, passing on the agent's final message or a file it lands?
open-question.recommendation: Each granted agent is verified doing its own shell-and-write work under its real contract, reading its procedure file and running its tool over a fixture milestone, so both keys and both agent-side path surfaces are checked at two dispatches, with no orchestrator layer whose failures would need transcript reading and no foreign task the agent's own instructions tell it to refuse.
open-question.alternative: Driver: minimal headless agy -p prompts that dispatch each agent directly with its real inputs, provide-alternatives-to-open-question with a Short Title, milestone directory, and scratch directory, and complete-task with the heading of one trivial fixture task. Agents covered: both. Pass signal: the files each agent lands, the alternatives scratch file holding <alternative> elements, and the fixture task's section moved from TASKS_TODO.md into TASKS_DONE.md by the task-list tool with the two paths staged. Both granted agents are verified doing their own shell-and-write work under their own contracts, without paying for or debugging the orchestrator skills, so each agent's key is checked on its own surface. The orchestrators' dispatch wording goes untested; the fixture must carry a task whose completion is cheap and deterministic, and the complete-task agent may still wander into real work or end FAILED: on content grounds; it depends on how the fixture workspace is seeded, which a sibling owns.

Driver: one headless agy -p run of /cairn:provide-alternatives-to-all-open-questions against a fixture milestone holding a small number of bare open questions. Agents covered: provide-alternatives-to-open-question only; complete-task is not exercised by the suite. Pass signal: the workflow's own end state, every fixture question carrying <alternative> elements in open_questions.xml and one Alternatives-annotation commit per question in the fixture repository's history. It reproduces the exact path that failed in the report (orchestrator, real dispatch prompt from the host's slot values, agent writing its scratch file and running the tool, batch embed and commit), so a pass means the reported failure is gone end to end rather than in a proxy. It is the slowest and costliest probe and fails for reasons unrelated to tool grants (a model drafting malformed XML, a repair skip, an orchestrator turn going wrong), so a red run needs transcript reading to tell a tool failure from a content failure; the complete-task agent's enable_write_tools key goes unverified; it needs a seeded git workspace, whose shape the fixture-workspace sibling owns.

Driver: two headless full-skill runs on a fixture milestone, /cairn:provide-alternatives-to-all-open-questions over bare questions and /cairn:complete-all-tasks over one trivial fixture task. Agents covered: both. Pass signal: the workflows' own end states, alternatives embedded in open_questions.xml with their Alternatives-annotation commits, and the task's section moved into TASKS_DONE.md with a Task-completion commit. Every agent that receives enable_write_tools is proven through the path users actually run, so neither key can silently go missing and both dispatch slot values are exercised with them. Roughly doubles the cost and flakiness of the full-pass probe, and a fixture task the complete-task agent can finish deterministically must be authored and maintained; content and orchestration failures still masquerade as tool failures; it depends on a fixture milestone that holds both questions and a task, a shape the fixture-workspace sibling owns.

Driver: a minimal headless agy -p prompt that tells the main agent to dispatch provide-alternatives-to-open-question with exactly its real inputs (a fixture Short Title, the fixture milestone directory, a scratch directory the suite created), bypassing the orchestrator skill and its batch. Agents covered: provide-alternatives-to-open-question only. Pass signal: the file the agent lands, <scratch dir>/<Short Title>.xml existing (no .xml.part left) and holding <alternative> elements, its content needing the agent's own python3 locate and list runs. It isolates the agent the report saw fail, with its real contract (shell calls to the open-question tool, a write and an mv), at a fraction of a full pass's cost and with no orchestrator batch or commit step that can fail for other reasons. The dispatch prompt is the suite's own wording, not the orchestrator's slot value, so a regression in how the skill dispatches is not caught; the result still depends on the model producing a usable alternative set; complete-task's key goes unverified.

Driver: minimal headless agy -p prompts that dispatch each of the two plugin agents with a trivial write-and-run task in place of its real inputs: write a small script holding a suite-generated nonce, run it with python3, and have the script write a marker file at a path the suite names. Agents covered: both. Pass signal: the marker file existing with the content only executing the written script could produce. It is the cheapest, most deterministic probe of exactly the property the fix grants (can this agent create a file and run a command), independent of the plugin's content, the model's drafting quality, git, or any milestone fixture, so a red run means a tool grant problem. The task contradicts each agent's own instructions (a fixed input contract and a DONE or FAILED: return), so the agent may refuse or end FAILED: and the probe partly tests instruction-following rather than tools; it does not exercise the plugin-root paths or tool commands the agents actually run, nor the real dispatch prompt, so a green probe says nothing about the reported workflow working.

Driver: the same trivial dispatch to each of the two agents, a script holding a suite-generated nonce written and run with python3. Agents covered: both. Pass signal: the headless run's final output (agy -p with --output-format text or json) reporting the script's printed result, with no file inspected. Needs no workspace path agreement or file inspection at all, so the suite is a prompt and a string comparison, the lightest harness of any option. The message passes through the main agent, which has its own write and shell tools and can produce the value itself when the subagent fails, so a pass does not prove the subagent ran anything; it shares the trivial-task option's conflict with the agents' own instructions and its blindness to the real paths and commands.

Driver: the same trivial write-and-run dispatch to each of the two agents. Agents covered: both. Pass signal: agy's own record of the run, the stream-json output or the subagent's transcript under ~/.gemini/antigravity-cli/brain, showing the subagent itself issuing successful file-write and command-run tool calls, rather than any outcome in the workspace. It asserts the exact thing the report diagnosed (the subagent had only view_file and send_message), attributing the tool calls to the subagent rather than the main agent, and holds even when the agent declines the foreign task partway. It parses an undocumented, version-specific record whose format and location agy may change in any release, so the suite breaks for reasons unrelated to the plugin; it shares the trivial task's blindness to the real workflow path.

Driver: two layers in the one suite, the trivial write-and-run dispatch to each of the two agents first, then one full /cairn:provide-alternatives-to-all-open-questions run on a fixture milestone. Agents covered: both by the trivial layer, the alternatives agent also end to end. Pass signal: the trivial layer's marker files with their nonce content, then the full layer's alternatives embedded in open_questions.xml with their Alternatives-annotation commits. A red trivial layer pins a failure on the tool grant cheaply and unambiguously, while the full layer proves the reported workflow actually runs, so the suite both diagnoses and confirms. It carries the full pass's cost and flakiness on every run plus a second harness to maintain, and the complete-task agent is still verified only by the trivial task, which conflicts with its own instructions; it needs the seeded fixture the fixture-workspace sibling owns.

open-question.question: Does the agy suite pin the model, effort, and print timeout it passes on each agy -p line, or run at the host's defaults with no --model, --effort, or --print-timeout as the headless chains in docs/ways-of-using-cairn.md do?
open-question.applied-principle: Check tier claims against the live environment
open-question.recommendation: Model and effort stay what the documented agy chains run, so a pass means the documented invocation works and no model id is held to go stale with the models list, while --print-timeout, a flag the installed CLI carries, ends a hung run with agy's own exit and output within a known time on the visible command line.
open-question.alternative: Every agy -p line carries no --model and no --effort, running at the account's defaults as the documented chains do, but carries one fixed --print-timeout value chosen by the suite, so agy itself ends any headless run that exceeds the bound. A hung run fails within a known time instead of blocking the suite, while the model and effort stay those a user's documented agy chain actually gets, so the suite still exercises the representative configuration. The model and effort still drift with the account's defaults, so runs are not reproducible; the one timeout value must fit a default model whose speed the suite does not control, so it is either loose enough to waste time on a hang or tight enough to cut a slow but correct run; the suite's lines no longer match the docs' lines token for token.

Every agy -p line the suite runs carries no --model, no --effort, and no --print-timeout, exactly like the agy lines in docs/ways-of-using-cairn.md, and the suite adds no wall-clock bound of its own: each headless process runs at the account's default model and effort and waits until its turn completes (agy's default --print-timeout of 0s). The suite runs exactly the command line a user's documented agy chain runs, so a pass means the documented invocation works, and the suite holds no model id or timeout value that can go stale when the agy models list or the host's speed changes. Results depend on whatever default model and effort the account has on the day, so two runs are not comparable and a failure may be the model's rather than the plugin's; a run that hangs (a subagent waiting on a tool it lacks, an auth prompt) hangs the suite until the invoker interrupts it by hand.

Every agy -p line carries no --model, no --effort, and no --print-timeout, identical in its flags to the documented agy lines, and the suite's own process launcher instead enforces a fixed wall-clock limit on each agy process, killing it and failing the test when the limit passes. Keeps the agy command line exactly the documented one while still bounding every run, and the bound also catches a hang that happens before agy's print loop starts (startup, plugin discovery, authentication), which --print-timeout may not cover. Model and effort drift with the account's defaults as in every defaults option; a killed process leaves no clean agy exit or final output to diagnose from, and the bound lives in harness code rather than on the visible command line, so its form depends on whether the suite is a pytest module or a standalone script (the axis the suite-location question owns).

Every agy -p line carries a fixed --model (a base model name from the agy models list) and a fixed --effort level that model offers, both literals in the suite, and no --print-timeout, with no wall-clock bound of the suite's own, so each run waits until its turn completes. Every run uses the same model and effort, so results are comparable across runs and machines and a failure points at the plugin or host integration rather than at a changed default, while the suite keeps the documented chains' unbounded wait that never cuts a slow but correct run. The pinned model id goes stale when the agy models list changes, and a run naming a model or effort the account lacks stops before testing anything; the suite's lines diverge from the documented defaults-only agy lines, so a pass no longer proves the default configuration works; a hang still blocks the suite until interrupted.

Every agy -p line carries a fixed --model, a fixed --effort level that model offers, and a fixed --print-timeout, all three literals in the suite, so each run is fully specified on its command line and agy ends any run that exceeds the bound. The most repeatable form: model, effort, and time limit are all fixed and visible on each line, so runs are comparable, a hang fails within a known time, and the timeout can be sized against one known model's speed rather than an unknown default's. Three literals to maintain: the model id goes stale with the agy models list and a missing model or effort stops the run, the timeout needs re-tuning when the pinned model changes, and the lines diverge furthest from the documented defaults-only agy lines, so the configuration users actually run is the one the suite never exercises.

Every agy -p line carries a fixed --model and a fixed --effort level that model offers, both literals in the suite, and no --print-timeout; the suite's own process launcher enforces a fixed wall-clock limit on each agy process, killing it and failing the test when the limit passes. Runs are reproducible on model and effort, and the bound covers every phase of the process, startup and plugin discovery included, without relying on how agy's own --print-timeout behaves. Carries the pinned model's staleness and missing-model stop, and a killed process leaves no clean agy exit or output to diagnose from; the bound lives in harness code whose form depends on whether the suite is a pytest module or a standalone script (the axis the suite-location question owns).

The suite passes no --model and no --effort unless the invoker supplies them (for example through environment variables the suite reads), in which case it passes the supplied values verbatim on every agy -p line; it passes a fixed default --print-timeout that the invoker may override the same way, an override of 0 restoring the unbounded wait. The default run matches the documented defaults-only invocation while never hanging, and a maintainer chasing a failure can pin a model and effort, or lift the bound, for one run without editing the suite, so no model id is hard-coded to go stale. Adds a configuration surface the suite must document and read, and a run's outcome depends on settings that appear nowhere in the suite's files, so a reported pass or failure means little unless the run also records which model, effort, and timeout it used.

open-question.question: Which plugin copy does the agy suite drive — the copy already installed at ~/.gemini/config/plugins/cairn as it stands, the freshly built hosts/antigravity/ tree that the suite installs over that path before running, or a copy installed under an isolated HOME the suite sets for the agy process so the user's own installation is never touched?
open-question.applied-principle: Check tier claims against the live environment
open-question.recommendation: Every run is guaranteed to test the current build at the real global path with the user's real credentials while writing nothing to the user's installation; the isolated-HOME and symlink forms rest on unverified host behaviour, the overwrite forms replace the user's install with a development tree, and the one extra copy step costs a command the stop line names.
open-question.alternative: Source: the copy already at ~/.gemini/config/plugins/cairn. Location: the user's real HOME. Install step: none, but before any agy process starts the suite compares that copy byte for byte with the repository's hosts/antigravity/ tree and stops on any difference, naming the remedy (re-extract or copy the built tree). It writes nothing to the user's installation. Every run is guaranteed to test the current build while the suite still never writes to the user's installation. Replacing the copy stays an explicit act of the user's own, and a stale install is caught rather than silently tested. Every build change makes the developer copy the tree by hand before the suite will run, which turns a one-command check into two steps. The comparison has to define which files count (the tree's README, .github workflow, and LICENSE ship too). How the suite reports a missing copy, as opposed to a different one, belongs to the sibling question on running without agy.

Source: the copy already at ~/.gemini/config/plugins/cairn, whatever release or build it holds. Location: the user's real HOME. Install step: none. The suite installs, compares, and restores nothing. It drives agy against that path and leaves keeping the copy current to the person running it. It is the simplest suite and never writes outside its fixture workspace. It exercises exactly the installation a user has, the same path the kinga_page failure ran against, and it can never disturb the user's own setup. A pass or fail says nothing about the change under test unless the user remembered to re-extract the freshly built tree first. Today the copy is a byte-identical 1.8.5 tree carrying the old .agents/plugins/cairn literal and no enable_write_tools key, so a run made after the milestone's build changes, with no reinstall, would test the old tree and report its old failures, or a stale pass.

Source: the freshly built hosts/antigravity/ tree. Location: the user's real HOME. Install step: before running, the suite replaces ~/.gemini/config/plugins/cairn with a copy of the built tree and leaves it there afterwards, with no backup or restore. One command always tests the current build, at the exact global path the milestone standardizes on, with the user's real agy credentials, trusted folders, and git identity. The resulting install is also the next release's tree, so the maintainer's own agy setup tracks the build. The suite silently overwrites the user's own installation with an unreleased build. Every other project the user runs agy in (kinga_page, for one) then loads that development tree until the user re-extracts a release, and a running agy session picks it up only on restart. A run on a contributor's machine replaces their installed release without asking.

Source: the freshly built hosts/antigravity/ tree. Location: the user's real HOME. Install step: the suite moves any existing ~/.gemini/config/plugins/cairn aside, copies the built tree into that path, runs, and on exit (pass, fail, or interrupt) removes its copy and moves the user's original back. If no copy stood there before, it leaves none behind. It tests the current build at the real global path with the user's real credentials and environment, and it leaves the user's installation as it found it once the run ends. While the suite runs, every agy session on the machine sees the development tree. A crash or kill between the move and the restore can strand the original under a backup name and leave the development tree installed. The suite also needs delete and move logic over a directory inside the user's own configuration, which is the riskiest code it would carry.

Source: the repository's hosts/antigravity/ tree itself, not a copy. Location: the user's real HOME. Install step: ~/.gemini/config/plugins/cairn is made a symbolic link to the checkout's hosts/antigravity/ (once by the developer, or by the suite whenever the path is not already that link) and stays in place, so every rebuild is live at the global path with no install step per run. The suite always drives the current build, and no copying happens on any run. The maintainer's agy picks up each rebuild the way their Claude Code setup already loads hosts/claude live. Whether agy resolves the link and reports the skill's absolute SKILL.md path as the repository location rather than ~/.gemini/config/plugins/cairn has not been verified. A suite meant to prove global plugin-root resolution could therefore pass against a path no user install ever has. Every agy session on the machine also loads uncommitted development state, and a user who installs releases is left with a link instead.

Source: the freshly built hosts/antigravity/ tree. Location: a temporary directory the suite creates and sets as HOME for each agy process. Install step: the suite copies the built tree to that directory's .gemini/config/plugins/cairn, and copies in the minimum agy needs to run (the OAuth credentials and account files under ~/.gemini, plus a git identity for the fixture's commits). It never writes to the user's real ~/.gemini. Every run tests the current build at the global path's real shape, relative to the HOME the process sees, and it never touches the user's installation or any running agy session. Leftover state from an earlier run or a stale workspace-local copy cannot leak in. Whether agy 1.4.0 derives its config root from HOME, and authenticates from copied oauth_creds.json alone without a keychain or a fresh login, is unverified. The suite would also copy live OAuth credentials into a temp directory. Changing HOME changes git config, uv caches, and anything else the run reads from it. Whether the tree's plugin-root literal resolves inside the isolated HOME depends on the sibling question on the plugin-root literal form.

open-question.question: Which surfaces does the suite's plugin-root resolution test cover — the orchestrator's file read of a shared procedure, its python3 tool command, and the same two inside a dispatched agent, or only the tool command — given that the report's failures showed up on both the file read and the command?
open-question.recommendation: Pins both failure modes the report observed in one dispatch-free process whose printed output asserts the read and the command separately, while the agent context's reads and commands are exercised by the subagent probe's real-input dispatches, whose landed files cannot appear without them; asserting an agent's read on its own would need a foreign prompt or an undocumented transcript format.
open-question.alternative: The resolution test covers the orchestrator only, on both surfaces: its file read of a shared procedure and its python3 tool command; no dispatched agent's resolution is asserted by this test. It pins both failure modes the report observed in the orchestrator — the view_file stat failure and python's exit 2 — in one headless agy process with no dispatch, keeping the test fast and its pass signal simple. The dispatched agent, whose prompt carries no plugin path and which never sees the absolute SKILL.md path the orchestrator receives, is exactly where a form that relies on that metadata would fail, and this test does not look there; agent-side resolution is then verified only if the subagent probe happens to exercise it, which depends on the shape that probe takes.

The resolution test covers all four surfaces in both rendered agents: the orchestrator's file read of a shared procedure and its python3 tool command, and inside each dispatched agent (provide-alternatives-to-open-question and complete-task) its own file read of a shared procedure (alternatives-procedure.md, complete-procedure.md) and its own tool command (open_questions.py, task_list.py), each surface asserted separately. Every place the report saw a path fail is pinned, and each agent's distinct procedure file and tool is exercised, so a literal form that resolves in the shell but not in the host's file-reading tool, or in the orchestrator but not in an agent whose prompt carries no plugin path, fails a named assertion rather than a later run. It is the costliest shape: at least two agent dispatches per run, each a slow headless agy process using model calls, and complete-task needs a fixture task it can complete; how cheaply the agent surfaces can be reached depends on the shape the subagent probe takes and the fixture workspace the suite uses.

The resolution test covers all four surfaces — the orchestrator's file read of a shared procedure and its python3 tool command, and the same two inside one dispatched agent (provide-alternatives-to-open-question, the agent the report observed failing) — and does not dispatch complete-task for resolution. Both failure surfaces are covered in both contexts the report distinguishes, including the agent whose prompt carries no plugin path, at the cost of a single agent dispatch; both agents' rendered literals come from the same plugin_root, so one agent stands in for the other's resolution. complete-task's own read of complete-procedure.md and its task_list.py command go unexercised, so a fault specific to that agent file's rendering or context is caught only by its write-tools probe, if that probe touches those paths; whether it does depends on the shape the subagent probe takes.

The resolution test covers the python3 tool command only, in both contexts: once run by the orchestrator and once run inside a dispatched agent; no file read of a shared procedure is asserted in either. A failed command is loud and mechanically checkable (a non-zero exit and a no-such-file line in the transcript or output), whereas a failed file read may be silently recovered by the model searching for the file, so the test keys on the unambiguous signal while still covering the agent context the orchestrator's metadata does not reach. The host's file-reading tool and the shell resolve paths differently (the shell expands a tilde or $HOME, a file-reading tool may not), so a literal form that passes the command check can still break every shared-procedure read; whether that gap matters depends on the literal form chosen for the plugin root.

The resolution test covers one surface in one context: the orchestrator's python3 tool command; neither file reads nor any dispatched agent is asserted. It is the smallest, fastest, and least flaky test: one headless agy process, no dispatch, and a pass signal (the tool's output or exit status) that needs no transcript inspection. It covers one of the four places the report's failures appeared, leaving the file-read surface and the agent context — the two places a literal form is most likely to resolve differently — to be caught only by a later real run; how much that leaves exposed depends on the literal form chosen for the plugin root.

The suite carries no separate resolution test: plugin-root resolution is treated as verified whenever the end-to-end subagent check passes, since that run cannot succeed unless the orchestrator's and the agent's reads and commands resolved; no surface is asserted on its own. It adds no extra agy process or assertion beyond what the suite already runs, keeping the on-demand suite as short and cheap as possible while still failing when resolution is broken. A failure reports only that the run failed, not which surface or context broke, and a model that recovers from a failed read by searching for the file can pass with a broken literal; whether the end-to-end check touches any given surface at all depends on the shape the subagent probe takes.

open-question.question: In what workspace does the agy suite run each headless agy process — a temporary git repository the suite seeds through the plugin's own tools with a milestone and open questions, a committed fixture directory under tests/fixtures/ copied to a temporary location, or the cairn repository checkout itself?
open-question.recommendation: A static, reviewable starting state in the copy-to-temp pattern the suite already uses, holding the bare questions and the one trivial task the direct dispatches need, so setup depends on no plugin tool being correct and a failure points at the host integration; a fixture gone stale is caught by the tools refusing it at run time.

The starting state is static, reviewable in a diff, and identical on every run, following the copy-to-tmp_path pattern the suite already uses, so the setup depends on no plugin tool being correct and a failure points at the host integration. The fixture is a second hand-maintained copy of the milestone layout: a later change to the file set or the XML form leaves it stale with nothing checking it, and the git initialisation still has to be scripted per run.

Each agy process runs in its own fresh git repository under the system temp location (a pytest tmp_path or a mktemp -d directory), which the suite builds at run time: git init, a milestones/README.md with its Current milestone: pointer written by the suite itself (no tool writes that file), the milestone directory created by define_milestone.py from a goal piped on stdin, its open questions appended by open_questions.py add, and an initial commit, all before the agy -p line runs with that directory as its working directory. The workspace is always in the exact layout and canonical XML form the current tools produce, so it can never drift from the milestone format the plugin expects, and every run starts from a clean, isolated, reproducible state that no earlier run or the cairn history can disturb. The seed is code to maintain: the question texts and goal live as strings in the suite, the README pointer is still hand-written, and a bug in define_milestone.py or open_questions.py breaks the agy suite's setup rather than surfacing as an Antigravity finding, which blurs what a failure means.

Each agy process runs with the cairn repository checkout itself as its working directory, against whatever milestone milestones/README.md currently points at, with no workspace created, copied, or seeded by the suite. No setup at all: the workspace is a real cairn-managed project with real milestones, so the run is as close to a user's use as the repository can offer. The runs write into the maintainer's own history: a committing skill lands Alternatives-annotation or other commits on the current milestone, the result depends on that milestone's live state (or fails outright when the pointer reads none), runs are not reproducible or isolable, and the checkout's own AGENTS.md and dirty working tree can steer or block the agent.

Each agy process runs in its own fresh, empty git repository under the system temp location, holding no milestones/ directory, pointer, or open questions; whatever a test needs (a file to write, a command to run) is named in its prompt rather than pre-seeded. The smallest possible workspace, with nothing to seed or maintain and no dependence on the milestone format, so the suite checks only plugin-root resolution and subagent tool execution and nothing else can fail it. It is viable only if the sibling questions on the subagent probe's shape and the resolution test's surfaces settle on probes that need no milestone; a full cairn skill run, or a python3 tool command over a milestone directory, has nothing to operate on here.

open-question.question: When the agy suite is invoked on a machine where agy is not on PATH or the global plugin copy it needs is absent, does it skip its tests, fail them, or stop before any test with one line naming the missing prerequisite?

An explicitly requested verification can never come back green on a machine that verified nothing. Aborting the run is only harmless if the suite is never collected as part of a broader run. Every suite test is skipped with a reason naming the missing prerequisite, and the run exits 0. That makes it harmless wherever the suite is collected on a machine without agy, CI's ubuntu job included, so the default run stays unchanged whatever the suite's location turns out to be. A run someone asked for on a misconfigured machine exits 0 with everything skipped, and the exit code reads as success. A contributor gate or release pre-flight that keys on the result can then pass without exercising agy at all, which defeats the point of a suite that runs only when someone wants the integration verified.

The suite is collected and run as normal, and each test (through a shared fixture or per-test guard) fails with a message naming the missing prerequisite. The run exits non-zero and reports one failure per test, and both prerequisites are treated the same way. It stays within ordinary per-test pytest machinery, needing no session-level abort hook, while still guaranteeing that a requested run on an unprepared machine cannot read as a pass. The report shows as many identical failures as the suite has tests, which buries the single real cause. It shares the stop option's hazard of turning any broader collection on a machine without agy red (the Suite location and invocation axis), with noisier output.

The two prerequisites are treated differently. When agy is not on PATH, every test is skipped with a reason naming agy and the run exits 0, because the machine simply cannot run the suite. When agy is present but the global plugin copy is absent, the run fails non-zero with a line naming the missing copy, because the installation this milestone standardizes on is missing on a machine set up for agy. The outcome follows what the absence means. A machine without the host is not a finding, while a host without the global install is exactly the kind of setup fault the global-path standardization is meant to rule out, so it is reported loudly. The split only makes sense if the suite drives the pre-installed global copy. If it installs its own copy, the second prerequisite never arises (the Suite plugin copy axis). It also keeps the skip option's risk that a requested run on a machine without agy exits 0, and it is two rules to document instead of one.

The suite skips with a reason naming the missing prerequisite and exits 0 by default. An explicit switch the suite documents (an environment variable or command-line flag) turns the same missing prerequisite into a stop before any test, with a non-zero exit and one line naming it. Both prerequisites get the same treatment in each mode. Any accidental or wholesale collection stays harmless, and a deliberate verification (a contributor gate or release pre-flight) can still demand that a missing prerequisite fail instead of passing silently. It adds a second mode and a switch that every invoking site must remember to set. A gate that forgets the flag silently falls back to the skip behaviour and its false green. It is also more mechanism than a suite that already runs only on request may need.

The suite adds no detection of either prerequisite. Its tests invoke agy and read the global copy directly, and on a machine lacking either they fail with whatever the subprocess or agy itself raises: a FileNotFoundError for a missing binary, or agy's own error or a failed resolution for a missing copy. The CLAUDE.md invariant is rewritten for Antigravity, or for any host with such a suite, to name the suite rather than a settings.toml block. Removes the hand-maintained prose record outright for this host. What is checked is whatever the suite asserts, re-verified on every run, so no dated block can say something the current host no longer does. The suite exercises plugin-root resolution and write and shell tools, not the dispatch, waiting, continuing, and context-file facts that sourced the eight slot values, so their provenance is lost unless the suite grows to cover them, which the goal does not ask for. The installed version checked leaves the committed record, since suite runs are not committed, and Antigravity's record then takes a different form from Codex's and Claude Code's.

The 2026-10-13 block against agy 1.3.4 is neither updated nor pointed at the suite: this milestone's checks go unrecorded in settings.toml, and the block stays a dated historical record of that earlier run. Changing it is left to a later milestone, or never done. At most, the clause tying it to "the plugin_root path below" is reworded so it no longer describes the new global path. No edit to the header and no CLAUDE.md change. A dated block that says what was checked on its date stays true as history, and the suite carries the new checks without any decision about how the two records relate. Goes against the invariant's own rule that a later re-check updates the block: this milestone's run is such a re-check, against a newer agy and a different install path, and it would leave no committed trace. The block would keep describing a workspace-relative install the milestone makes unsupported, misleading the next editor about which version and which layout the slot values were last confirmed against.
